readings.title: A bus connection after work
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
An evening bus reached the station just before a train left. Workers complained that the connection rarely worked in practice. The main obstacle was a timetable with no walking allowance. The printed arrival time assumed that passengers could cross the station instantly. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used records of actual bus and walking times. Planners followed the route over several evenings and counted missed connections. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated a small schedule shift made the transfer possible. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a later train connection shown in route guidance. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: a timetable should reflect a whole journey. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in a bus connection after work, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Deliveries to a narrow street
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Several shops on a narrow street received parcels during the lunch rush. Vans sometimes stopped across the pedestrian crossing. The main obstacle was unloading without a shared time plan. Drivers chose the nearest available space even when a safe bay stood farther away. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used delivery counts by hour and shop. Traders and drivers compared busy periods and checked the distance to the legal loading bay. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated most deliveries could avoid the lunch period. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced coordinated delivery windows and clearer bay signs. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: efficient delivery must respect street safety. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in deliveries to a narrow street, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Finding a cycle route at night
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Cyclists used a marked route across a park. At dusk, some missed a turn and entered an unlit service road. The main obstacle was direction signs visible only in daylight. The arrow used low contrast and stood behind branches from the usual approach. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a supervised evening route check. The council invited riders to identify junctions while noting sight lines without placing anyone at risk. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated one junction caused most wrong turns. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced reflective signs at the decision point. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: route information must work in actual conditions. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in finding a cycle route at night, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Sharing a parcel collection point
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A housing block introduced a secure parcel room. Residents liked it, but weekend collections formed a line outside the entrance. The main obstacle was a short collection period for many households. The room was open only when one staff member was present on Saturday morning. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a review of collection logs. Managers compared arrival times and asked residents which alternatives would be practical. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated extended access mattered more than more space. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced two shorter opening periods on different days. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: service design should match user schedules. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in sharing a parcel collection point, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
When a community changes the local transport coordination programme, a short explanation can be as important as the change itself. People want to know what problem was noticed, how information was gathered and why one option was selected. For a project about transport and local delivery, staff observed actual use rather than relying only on a drawing or an early promise. The evidence revealed an obstacle that was not obvious at first. Organizers made a limited adjustment and told residents when it would be reviewed. They also described the limits of the trial, because a small number of visits cannot represent every future situation. An honest account made the decision easier to question and improve.

translation.referenceAnswer: 社区调整一项服务时，简短解释可能和改动本身同样重要。人们想知道发现了什么问题、如何收集信息，以及为何选择某个方案。在一个有关交通组织与配送的项目中，工作人员观察实际使用，而不只依靠图纸或最初的承诺。证据揭示了起初并不明显的障碍。组织者作出有限调整，并告知居民何时重新评估。他们也说明试行的局限，因为少量使用经历不能代表未来所有情况。诚实的说明让这项决定更容易被讨论和改进。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the transport planning team suggesting a practical change to the local transport coordination programme. Describe who should be consulted, how the change could be tried, and when it should be reviewed.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the local transport coordination programme. People have noticed a timetable with no walking allowance, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
